Fixed at one point of sky

questions.question: Q1. State Newton's law of gravitation.
questions.answer: Every particle attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance: F = GMm/r², along the line joining their centres.
questions.example: Doubling r quarters the gravitational force.

questions.question: Q2. Define gravitational field strength and find it at Earth's surface.
questions.answer: Gravitational field strength is the force per unit mass at a point: g = F/m = GM/r². At Earth's surface, g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 N/kg.
questions.example: Field is strongest at the surface, weaker with altitude.

questions.question: Q3. Find G from given g, M and R of Earth.
questions.answer: G = gR²/M. Using g = 9.8, R = 6.4×10⁶ m, M = 6×10²⁴ kg: G ≈ 6.7×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

questions.question: Q4. How does the gravitational force between two bodies change if their distance is halved?
questions.answer: Since F ∝ 1/r², halving the distance multiplies the force by (2)² = 4. ▥ 7.1–7.2 Law of Gravitation & Field Strength  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Gravitational Field Intensity vs Potential ▣ 7.3 Gravitational Potential & Energy
questions.example: Closer objects attract much more strongly.

questions.question: Q5. Define gravitational potential and potential energy at a point.
questions.answer: Gravitational potential is the work done per unit mass bringing a unit mass from infinity to the point: V = −GM/r. Potential energy of mass m: U = mV = −GMm/r (negative, zero at infinity).
questions.example: Closer to a mass → more negative potential.

questions.question: Q6. Why is gravitational potential energy negative?
questions.answer: Zero is defined at infinity. Since gravity is attractive, work must be done against it to bring a mass from infinity to a point, so the stored potential energy is less than zero (negative).
questions.shortcut: Reference U=0 at ∞; attraction makes it negative.
questions.example: A bound orbit has negative total energy.

questions.question: Q7. Find the gravitational potential at Earth's surface.
questions.answer: V = −GM/R² × R = −gR = −9.8×6.4×10⁶ ≈ −6.27×10⁷ J/kg. ▥ 7.3 Gravitational Potential & Energy  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Gravitational Potential vs Potential Energy ▣ 7.4 Variation of g with Altitude & Depth

questions.question: Q8. How does g vary with altitude? Derive g(h)=g₀(1−h/R).
questions.answer: At height h, g(h) = GM/(R+h)². For h ≪ R, g(h) ≈ g₀(1 − h/R). So g decreases with altitude.
questions.example: At h = R, g becomes g₀/4.

questions.question: Q9. How does g vary with depth? Derive g(d)=g₀(1−d/R).
questions.answer: Only the mass within the sphere of radius (R−d) contributes: g(d) = g₀(R−d)/R = g₀(1−d/R). It falls linearly to zero at the centre.
questions.shortcut: g(d) = g₀(1−d/R); g=0 at the core.
questions.example: At depth R/2, g = g₀/2.

questions.question: Q10. At what height does g reduce to half its surface value?
questions.answer: g(h)=g₀/2 → 1/(1+h/R)² = ½ → 1+h/R = √2 → h = (√2−1)R ≈ 0.414R ≈ 2650 km. ▥ 7.4 Variation of g with Altitude & Depth  —  Compare / Contrast Tables g at Poles vs Equator g with Altitude vs with Depth ▣ 7.5 Centre of Mass & Centre of Gravity
questions.example: ≈ 2650 km above the surface.

questions.question: Q11. Define centre of mass and centre of gravity.
questions.answer: Centre of mass: point where the whole mass may be considered concentrated, R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ/Σmᵢ. Centre of gravity: point through which the total weight acts. In a uniform gravitational field they coincide.
questions.shortcut: x_cm = Σmᵢxᵢ/M ; CG = COM when g uniform.
questions.example: A uniform rod: COM at its midpoint.

questions.question: Q12. Find the centre of mass of two masses 2 kg at x=0 and 3 kg at x=5 m.
questions.answer: x_cm = (2×0 + 3×5)/(2+3) = 15/5 = 3 m from the origin.
questions.example: Sits at x = 3 m.

questions.question: Q13. Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform triangular lamina?
questions.answer: At the centroid, the intersection of the medians, located ⅓ of the altitude from the base (⅔ from the vertex). ▥ 7.5 Centre of Mass & Centre of Gravity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Centre of Mass vs Centre of Gravity ▣ 7.6–7.7 Satellite Motion & Escape Velocity
questions.example: A uniform rod's CG is at its midpoint.

questions.question: Q14. Find the orbital velocity of a satellite just above Earth's surface.
questions.answer: mv²/r = GMm/r² → v = √(GM/r). At r = R: v = √(gR) ≈ √(9.8×6.4×10⁶) ≈ 7900 m/s ≈ 7.9 km/s (first cosmic velocity).
questions.example: ≈ 7.9 km/s at low orbit.

questions.question: Q15. Derive the time period of a satellite T = 2π√(r³/GM).
questions.answer: Centripetal force from gravity: mv²/r = GMm/r² → v = √(GM/r). Period T = circumference/speed = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM).
questions.example: Higher orbit → longer period.

questions.question: Q16. Derive the escape velocity v_e = √(2gR).
questions.answer: Total energy at surface = ½mv_e² − GMm/R. To escape, set final energy ≥ 0: ½mv_e² = GMm/R → v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s.
questions.example: Faster than circular speed by √2.

questions.question: Q17. Relation between escape and orbital velocity at the surface.
questions.answer: v_e/v_orbit = √(2gR)/√(gR) = √2. So escape velocity is √2 times the (low) orbital velocity. ▥ 7.6–7.7 Satellite Motion & Escape Velocity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Geostationary vs Polar (Sun-synchronous) Satellite ▣ 7.8–7.10 Satellite Energy, Geostationary & GPS

questions.question: Q18. Find the total energy of a satellite in orbit and its KE and PE.
questions.answer: For circular orbit: KE = GMm/2r, PE = −GMm/r, so Total E = −GMm/2r. Total energy is negative (bound system); KE = −(Total E).
questions.example: Higher orbit → less (less negative) total energy.

questions.question: Q19. What is a geostationary satellite? State its features.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in the equatorial plane in the same direction, with period equal to Earth's rotation (24 h), appearing fixed over one point. Orbit height ≈ 36 000 km, radius ≈ 42 200 km.
questions.shortcut: T=24 h, r≈42 200 km, over equator.
questions.example: Used for TV & weather (e.g. GEO satellites).

questions.question: Q20. How does GPS work and why are many satellites needed?
questions.answer: GPS uses a constellation of satellites (usually 24+, in 3 orbital planes). Each transmits a timed signal; a receiver measures time-of-arrival from ≥4 satellites to trilaterate its position (3 for position, the 4th for the clock offset). ▥ 7.8–7.10 Satellite Energy, Geostationary & GPS  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Orbital Energy Table (circular orbit) PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Measure travel-time × c to each satellite → position; need ≥4.
questions.example: Your phone fixes a location using several GPS sats.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive g in terms of G, M and R of the Earth.
theoryItems.answer: The gravitational force on mass m at the surface equals its weight: G M m/R² = mg → g = GM/R². Hence the surface gravitational field strength follows from Earth's mass and radius.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive g(h) = g₀(1 − h/R) at altitude.
theoryItems.answer: g(h) = GM/(R+h)² = g₀(R²/(R+h)²). For h ≪ R, (R+h)² ≈ R²(1+2h/R) → g(h) ≈ g₀(1 − h/R), so g decreases with height.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T3. Derive g(d) = g₀(1 − d/R) at depth.
theoryItems.answer: Only the mass of the sphere of radius (R−d) contributes (shell theorem): g(d) = G·[4/3π(R−d)³ρ] / (R−d)² = g₀(R−d)/R = g₀(1 − d/R). Linear to zero at the centre.
theoryItems.example: At the core g = 0; at R/2 depth g = g₀/2.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T4. Derive the escape velocity and its relation to orbital velocity.
theoryItems.answer: Escape: total energy = ½mv² − GMm/r set ≥ 0 → v_e = √(2GM/r) = √(2gR) at the surface ≈ 11.2 km/s. Ratio to the circular (orbital) speed = √2.
theoryItems.example: A satellite must reach 11.2 km/s to escape Earth.

theoryItems.question: [State] T5. State Newton's law of universal gravitation and the value of G.
theoryItems.answer: Every particle attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance: F = Gm₁m₂/r². G ≈ 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² (measured by Cavendish).

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain how Cavendish measured G.
theoryItems.answer: Two small lead masses were brought near two larger ones on a torsion balance; the tiny gravitational torque twisted a fine fibre. Knowing the masses and the twist (via a light beam), the force — and hence G — was found. This 'weighed the Earth.'
theoryItems.shortcut: Torsion balance: measure the tiny twist → G.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the centre of mass and centre of gravity, and when they differ.
theoryItems.answer: Centre of mass: point where the whole mass can be concentrated, R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ/Σmᵢ. Centre of gravity: point where total weight acts. In a uniform gravitational field they coincide; in a non-uniform field they can separate.
theoryItems.example: An extended body in Earth's field is nearly at the same point.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain the motion of a satellite: orbital velocity and time period.
theoryItems.answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r → v = √(GM/r). Period T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM), which is Kepler's third law (T² ∝ r³).
theoryItems.example: Low orbit: v ≈ 7.9 km/s; higher orbit slower & longer.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T9. Explain a geostationary satellite and its characteristics.
theoryItems.answer: Orbits Earth in the equatorial plane, prograde, with a period equal to Earth's rotation (≈24 h / 86 400 s), so it appears fixed over one point. Radius ≈ 42 200 km (altitude ≈ 36 000 km).
theoryItems.shortcut: T = 24 h; r ≈ 42 200 km; over equator.
theoryItems.example: Used for communications and weather over a fixed region.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T10. Explain how GPS works and why multiple satellites are needed.
theoryItems.answer: GPS uses a constellation of satellites (typically 24+) in 3 planes. Each transmits a time-stamped signal; a receiver measures the travel time to each satellite to trilaterate its position (3 satellites give position, a 4th corrects the receiver clock).
theoryItems.example: Your phone fixes a location from several GPS satellites.

▣ 7.1–7.2 Law of Gravitation & Field Strength
Q1. State Newton's law of gravitation.

Answer:  Every particle attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance: F = GMm/r², along the line joining their centres.
⚡ Shortcut:  F = GMm/r² (inverse-square, always attractive).
Example:  Doubling r quarters the gravitational force.
Q2. Define gravitational field strength and find it at Earth's surface.
Answer:  Gravitational field strength is the force per unit mass at a point: g = F/m = GM/r². At Earth's surface, g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 N/kg.
⚡ Shortcut:  g = GM/r² (N/kg = m/s²).
Example:  Field is strongest at the surface, weaker with altitude.
Q3. Find G from given g, M and R of Earth.
Answer:  G = gR²/M. Using g = 9.8, R = 6.4×10⁶ m, M = 6×10²⁴ kg: G ≈ 6.7×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².
⚡ Shortcut:  G = gR²/M.
Example:  ≈ 6.7×10⁻¹¹ (SI).
Q4. How does the gravitational force between two bodies change if their distance is halved?
Answer:  Since F ∝ 1/r², halving the distance multiplies the force by (2)² = 4.
⚡ Shortcut:  Inverse-square: (2)² = 4×, (3)² = 9×.
Example:  Closer objects attract much more strongly.

Q5. Define gravitational potential and potential energy at a point.
Answer:  Gravitational potential is the work done per unit mass bringing a unit mass from infinity to the point: V = −GM/r. Potential energy of mass m: U = mV = −GMm/r (negative, zero at infinity).
⚡ Shortcut:  V = −GM/r ; U = −GMm/r.
Example:  Closer to a mass → more negative potential.
Q6. Why is gravitational potential energy negative?
Answer:  Zero is defined at infinity. Since gravity is attractive, work must be done against it to bring a mass from infinity to a point, so the stored potential energy is less than zero (negative).
⚡ Shortcut:  Reference U=0 at ∞; attraction makes it negative.
Example:  A bound orbit has negative total energy.
Q7. Find the gravitational potential at Earth's surface.
⚡ Shortcut:  V_surface = −gR.

Q8. How does g vary with altitude? Derive g(h)=g₀(1−h/R).
Answer:  At height h, g(h) = GM/(R+h)². For h ≪ R, g(h) ≈ g₀(1 − h/R). So g decreases with altitude.
⚡ Shortcut:  g(h) = g₀(1−h/R) (small h).
Example:  At h = R, g becomes g₀/4.
Q9. How does g vary with depth? Derive g(d)=g₀(1−d/R).
Answer:  Only the mass within the sphere of radius (R−d) contributes: g(d) = g₀(R−d)/R = g₀(1−d/R). It falls linearly to zero at the centre.
⚡ Shortcut:  g(d) = g₀(1−d/R); g=0 at the core.
Example:  At depth R/2, g = g₀/2.
Q10. At what height does g reduce to half its surface value?
⚡ Shortcut:  h = (√2−1)R for half g.

▣ 7.5 Centre of Mass & Centre of Gravity
Q11. Define centre of mass and centre of gravity.

Answer:  Centre of mass: point where the whole mass may be considered concentrated, R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ/Σmᵢ. Centre of gravity: point through which the total weight acts. In a uniform gravitational field they coincide.
⚡ Shortcut:  x_cm = Σmᵢxᵢ/M ; CG = COM when g uniform.
Example:  A uniform rod: COM at its midpoint.
Q12. Find the centre of mass of two masses 2 kg at x=0 and 3 kg at x=5 m.
Answer:  x_cm = (2×0 + 3×5)/(2+3) = 15/5 = 3 m from the origin.
⚡ Shortcut:  x_cm = Σmx/M.
Example:  Sits at x = 3 m.
Q13. Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform triangular lamina?
Answer:  At the centroid, the intersection of the medians, located ⅓ of the altitude from the base (⅔ from the vertex).
⚡ Shortcut:  Triangle CG = centroid (1/3 from base).
Example:  A uniform rod's CG is at its midpoint.

▣ 7.6–7.7 Satellite Motion & Escape Velocity
Q14. Find the orbital velocity of a satellite just above Earth's surface.
Answer:  mv²/r = GMm/r² → v = √(GM/r). At r = R: v = √(gR) ≈ √(9.8×6.4×10⁶) ≈ 7900 m/s ≈ 7.9 km/s (first cosmic velocity).
⚡ Shortcut:  v_orbit = √(gR²/r) = √(GM/r).
Example:  ≈ 7.9 km/s at low orbit.
Q15. Derive the time period of a satellite T = 2π√(r³/GM).
Answer:  Centripetal force from gravity: mv²/r = GMm/r² → v = √(GM/r). Period T = circumference/speed = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM).
⚡ Shortcut:  T = 2π√(r³/GM); T² ∝ r³ (Kepler).
Example:  Higher orbit → longer period.
Q16. Derive the escape velocity v_e = √(2gR).
Answer:  Total energy at surface = ½mv_e² − GMm/R. To escape, set final energy ≥ 0: ½mv_e² = GMm/R → v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s.
⚡ Shortcut:  v_e = √2 · v_orbit(surface) = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s.
Example:  Faster than circular speed by √2.
Q17. Relation between escape and orbital velocity at the surface.
Answer:  v_e/v_orbit = √(2gR)/√(gR) = √2. So escape velocity is √2 times the (low) orbital velocity.
⚡ Shortcut:  v_e = √2 × v_orbit.
Example:  ≈ 11.2 vs 7.9 km/s.

Q18. Find the total energy of a satellite in orbit and its KE and PE.
Answer:  For circular orbit: KE = GMm/2r, PE = −GMm/r, so Total E = −GMm/2r. Total energy is negative (bound system); KE = −(Total E).
⚡ Shortcut:  KE = +GMm/2r, PE = −GMm/r, E_total = −GMm/2r.
Example:  Higher orbit → less (less negative) total energy.
Q19. What is a geostationary satellite? State its features.

Answer:  A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in the equatorial plane in the same direction, with period equal to Earth's rotation (24 h), appearing fixed over one point. Orbit height ≈ 36 000 km, radius ≈ 42 200 km.
⚡ Shortcut:  T=24 h, r≈42 200 km, over equator.
Example:  Used for TV & weather (e.g. GEO satellites).
Q20. How does GPS work and why are many satellites needed?

Answer:  GPS uses a constellation of satellites (usually 24+, in 3 orbital planes). Each transmits a timed signal; a receiver measures time-of-arrival from ≥4 satellites to trilaterate its position (3 for position, the 4th for the clock offset).
⚡ Shortcut:  Measure travel-time × c to each satellite → position; need ≥4.
Example:  Your phone fixes a location using several GPS sats.
